title: What accounting helps us decide
goal: Identify the users of accounting information and the different questions answered by the four course statements.

slides.title: What can the accounts tell a business owner?

items.heading: Position
items.text: What do we own and owe?

slides.lead: Summit Trail Co. provides outdoor services and sells equipment.
slides.takeaway: A bank balance answers only part of the question.
slides.notes: Fictional teaching company, separate from assessed datasets. Ask what a lender would want to know.

slides.title: Accounting turns evidence into useful information

items.heading: Identify
items.text: Find a measurable event and its evidence.

items.heading: Record
items.text: Translate the event into accounts and amounts.

slides.takeaway: Reliable reports depend on reliable records.
slides.notes: Examples of evidence: invoices, receipts, payroll records, bank records, contracts. Not every document requires an entry.

slides.title: Keep the business separate from its owners

rows: An owner invests in company shares
Each party records its own side

slides.notes: Even a sole proprietor separates personal and business records for accounting.

slides.title: Business forms explain the equity terminology
slides.takeaway: Our recurring case is a corporation.
slides.notes: Keep legal and tax details outside this comparison. Common Stock is a simplified contributed-capital account.

slides.title: Different users ask different questions

items.heading: Managers
items.text: Which activity earns enough to continue? Can we hire another employee?

items.heading: Outside users
items.text: Lenders ask about repayment. Investors consider return and risk.

slides.takeaway: Different users ask different questions of the same records.

slides.title: Four statements tell connected parts of the story

rows: What profit or loss did we earn?
What are our assets, liabilities, and equity?
Why did cash increase or decrease?

slides.notes: Published company reports may show a broader statement of changes in shareholders’ equity.

slides.title: A balance sheet is a snapshot; other statements cover a period

items.heading: At June 30
items.text: The balance sheet shows balances at one date.

items.heading: For the month ended June 30
items.text: Income, retained earnings, and cash flows cover a period.

slides.takeaway: Check the company, date or period, and currency.

slides.title: Try it: cash in, cash out, and the ending balance
slides.lead: Find ending cash. Can you also calculate profit?
slides.notes: The receipt could be borrowing or revenue; the payment could buy an asset or pay an expense.

blocks.text: Profit remains unknown. We need to know what the receipt and payment were for.

slides.title: Course workflow and exit check

items.heading: Accounts
items.text: Post and prepare a trial balance.

slides.lead: Exit check: which statement helps investigate a cash shortage?
slides.notes: Introduce the five assignment milestones. Keep team setup and submission dates in the assignment instructions.

blocks.text: Start with cash flows; then examine receivables, inventory, and obligations on the balance sheet.
